items.prompt: What is interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC)?
items.answer: Interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC) is a staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical usability evaluation.

Design is the interface and interaction design part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle in interactive system development, not code design, that may be based on intuition, design guidelines, or team brainstorming, and is refined through prototyping and quick evaluation until stable.

Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

questions.question: At what point is the final usability evaluation of the whole system performed in an interactive system lifecycle?
options: After the feasibility study approves the idea
After the final prototype is accepted as usable
After code testing shows the system runs smoothly
After the requirements are signed off by the client
questions.explanation: The whole system is empirically evaluated for usability after implementation and code testing have made it run smoothly. Prototype acceptance or early requirement sign-off does not make the full system ready for final usability evaluation.

questions.question: What signals that the prototype and evaluation loop can stop?
options: When the design has stabilized
When the bugs have been removed
When the code has compiled
When the final evaluation is finished
questions.explanation: The loop is repeated as evaluation results refine the design, and it ends when that design stabilizes. Compilation, bug removal, or final evaluation belong to later stages, not the design refinement cycle.

questions.question: Which part of an XR project can be handled like ordinary software development?
options: Prototyping and quick evaluation are standard SDLC stages
Coding and code testing are standard SDLC stages
Usability evaluation and prototyping are standard SDLC stages
Interface design and prototyping are standard SDLC stages
questions.explanation: Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and system evaluation follow standard software development practice, so they are not treated as XR-specific techniques. Prototyping and quick evaluation support design decisions, but they do not replace code testing or fix the final interface by themselves.

questions.question: Which cycle may be frequent even though other cycles are kept infrequent?
options: The requirement-gathering and design cycle
The coding and code-testing cycle
The design-prototype-evaluation cycle
The feasibility and coding cycle
questions.explanation: The design-prototype-evaluation cycle may be repeated often as the design is refined, while other back-and-forth cycles are generally kept infrequent to avoid cost and time overrun.

data.text: System implementation sits in the interactive system development lifecycle, which also applies to XR systems. That lifecycle moves from feasibility and requirements through a design-prototype-quick-evaluation cycle, then standard coding and testing, and finally whole-system usability evaluation. The design-prototype-evaluate cycle can repeat until the design stabilizes, while other cycles are kept generally infrequent to avoid cost and time overrun.
points: Usability evaluation is the empirical evaluation of the whole system from the usability point of view in interactive system development.
The interactive system development lifecycle applies to XR systems and includes feasibility, requirements, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle, coding, testing, and usability evaluation.
The design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle that repeats until the design stabilizes.
Code design, coding, implementation, and code testing are standard software development lifecycle stages with nothing VR or AR specific.
Other cycles can connect coding, testing, evaluation, and requirements, but should generally be infrequent to avoid cost and time overrun.

activities.title: Order the stages of the interactive system development lifecycle

items.title: Order the stages of the interactive system development lifecycle
steps: Iterating design, prototyping and quick evaluation
Designing, coding and implementing the system
Testing the code and the system
Evaluating the whole system for usability

questions.question: What is the design-prototype-evaluate cycle mainly a loop of?
options: Prototyping, evaluating, and refining the design
Coding, testing, and releasing the system
Gathering, analyzing, and approving requirements
Specifying, budgeting, and procuring hardware
questions.explanation: The cycle repeatedly builds a quick prototype of the design, evaluates it, finds problems, and refines the design until it stabilizes. Coding, requirements approval, and hardware procurement are separate parts of the wider development process.

questions.question: In the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, what does the term design refer to?
options: Interface and code design
Interface and interaction design
Code and implementation design
Interaction and requirement design
questions.explanation: In this cycle, design means the interface and interaction design, not the design of the code or implementation. Code design and implementation belong to later, standard software development stages.

questions.question: Why is a quick usability evaluation technique required in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle?
options: To fit code design into the prototype before any user testing
To fit each prototype into the final product without further evaluation
To fit many cycles into a reasonable timeframe without cost overrun
To fit requirement gathering into the design before any prototype
questions.explanation: Quick usability evaluation lets the many design-prototype-evaluate cycles stay within a reasonable timeframe and avoids cost overrun. A prototype is not automatically the final product, and the cycle is not a substitute for code design or requirement gathering.

questions.question: What does a quick evaluation of a design idea require in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle?
options: A design guideline and a quick evaluation method
A quickly buildable prototype and a final usability report
A quickly buildable prototype and a quick evaluation method
A fully implemented system and a quick evaluation method
questions.explanation: Quick evaluation needs both a prototype that can be built fast and an evaluation method that is also quick. A full implementation is too heavy for fast cycling, a final report is not an evaluation method, and design guidelines alone do not test a design idea.

data.text: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design repeatedly designs, quickly prototypes, evaluates, finds problems, and refines until the design stabilizes, with design meaning interface and interaction design, not code design. Many iterations make speed important, so quick usability evaluation is required to keep the work within reasonable time and cost and to make implemented ideas usable. For that evaluation to be quick, a quickly built design prototype and a quick evaluation method are both needed and equally important.
points: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design repeats designing, quickly prototyping, evaluating, finding problems, and refining until stabilized.
In the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, design means interface and interaction design, not code design.
Quick usability evaluation keeps cycles within reasonable time and cost, prevents cost overrun, and makes implemented ideas usable.
Quick evaluation of design ideas needs a quickly built design prototype and a quick evaluation method, both equally important.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of using a prototype for an untested design idea?
options: It is lightweight and can document a full implementation in practice
It is lightweight and can replace a full implementation in practice
It is lightweight and can prove that the idea works in practice
It is lightweight and can test whether the idea works in practice
questions.explanation: A prototype is a lightweight implementation used to test whether a design idea works in practice. Proving, replacing, or documenting a full implementation is not its defining purpose.

questions.question: In the best case, what can happen to a prototype after it has served its testing purpose?
options: It can be replaced by design guidelines once its testing purpose has been served
It can be refined and tested until it becomes the final product
It can be archived as a usability report once its testing purpose has been served
It can be discarded once its testing purpose has been served
questions.explanation: A prototype may be discarded, but in the best case it is incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it becomes the fully implemented final product. Discarding it is not the best-case outcome.

questions.question: Why must a design be implemented and tested rather than judged only from design guidelines?
options: Design guidelines finish a design and do not show whether it is usable
Design guidelines only start a design and do show whether it is usable
Design guidelines only start a design and do not show whether it is usable
Design guidelines finish a design and do show whether it is usable
questions.explanation: Design guidelines are only a starting point; they do not indicate whether a design is usable, so the design must be implemented and tested to determine whether it will work. Saying they finish a design or show usability is false.

data.text: Design guidelines are only a starting point, so a design must be implemented and tested to determine whether it works. A prototype gives a quick, lightweight way to test a design idea with far fewer resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, whose failure wastes money and time. After testing, a prototype can be discarded, or in the best case it can be incrementally evolved into the final product.
points: Prototyping techniques support quick prototype building and evaluation to collect usability feedback on design ideas.
Design guidelines are only a starting point, so designs need implementation and testing to determine whether they work.
A prototype is a lightweight implementation for testing design ideas needing fewer resources, skilled manpower, and cost than full implementation.
A full software implementation needs skilled programmers, resources, and cost, so a bad idea wastes money and time.
A prototype can be discarded after testing, or in the best case incrementally evolved into the final product.

questions.question: What kind of user feedback is a horizontal prototype suitable for collecting?
options: feedback on the performance and reliability of commonly used features
feedback on the interactions and screen changes in a selected task
feedback on the look, feel, and appearance of the whole interface
feedback on the sequence of screens and states in a complete workflow
questions.explanation: A horizontal prototype presents the interface’s appearance without real functionality or interaction, so it is used to discuss and elicit feedback about how the interface looks, feels, and appears. Feedback about task interactions, performance, or screen sequences belongs to deeper, interaction-bearing prototypes.

questions.question: Why does a vertical prototype implement a few selected features in depth rather than every feature?
options: because doing that for every feature would require a different display
because doing that for every feature would make it too expensive
because doing that for every feature would amount to the full system
because doing that for every feature would hide the main interactions
questions.explanation: A vertical prototype implements selected features in depth, but not all features, because covering every feature would already be the full system. Cost, display requirements, or hiding interactions are not the reason for this scope limit.

questions.question: Which pair of things can the word “screen” cover in a vertical prototype?
options: a 2D computer screen and a printed storyboard
a 2D computer screen and a virtual scene
a paper storyboard and a three-dimensional print
a virtual scene and a physical model of an interface
questions.explanation: In this context, “screen” is generic: it can mean a two-dimensional computer screen or a scene in a virtual or immersive environment. Paper storyboards, physical models, and three-dimensional prints are not what the term “screen” refers to here.

data.text: Horizontal and vertical prototypes are distinguished by the aspect of the interface they represent. A horizontal prototype presents the whole interface at a surface level, without functionality, so it can be used to gather feedback on its appearance. A vertical prototype instead implements selected common features in depth, from first to last screen, and therefore supports analysis of interactions and features. In this vertical prototype context, the terms implemented and screen are used generically.
points: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories: horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.
A horizontal prototype depicts the entire interface at surface level, with no functionality, for user feedback on appearance.
A vertical prototype implements a few selected likely common features in depth, not all, from first to last screen.
Vertical prototypes are suitable for analysis of interactions and features because they implement interactions.
In vertical prototypes, implemented need not mean code, and screen can be a 2D computer screen or an immersive scene.

questions.question: What distinguishes a low-fidelity prototype from a coded prototype?
options: a simple animation tool without real software for the prototype
a reduced-scale program with limited functionality for the prototype
a computer without programming code for the prototype
non-digital materials such as paper or cardboard for the prototype
questions.explanation: A low-fidelity prototype is made without a computer, code, or programming, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood. Digital mockups, reduced-scale programs, and animation tools are not low-fidelity in this sense.

questions.question: Why is low-fidelity prototyping useful early in interface design?
options: It is a quick and inexpensive way to render a virtual environment for review
It is a quick and inexpensive way to compare interface ideas and collect usability feedback
It is a quick and inexpensive way to test coded interactions under load
It is a quick and inexpensive way to verify every feature of the final system
questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototyping is mainly used for fast, cheap brainstorming and user feedback on usability, not for testing coded interaction, full final functionality, or rendered virtual environments.

questions.question: What can a storyboard show that a single interface sketch cannot?
options: the order of user actions and the screen changes needed to complete a task
the complete working functionality of every feature in the system from the first action to the last
the final polished appearance of each interface element in detail
the full virtual environment with all objects in their final positions and scale
questions.explanation: A single sketch gives a static view of one interface, while a storyboard uses a series of keyframes to capture the sequence of actions and corresponding screens for a task. It does not imply complete working functionality, a full virtual environment, or final polished detail.

questions.question: What does evaluation of an early interface sketch allow the design to do?
options: change elements, appearance, position, or layout after feedback
keep the elements, appearance, position, or layout after feedback
repeat the elements, appearance, position, or layout after feedback
copy the elements, appearance, position, or layout after feedback
questions.explanation: Prototypes are made to be evaluated and revised, so an early sketch is not a fixed final design. Feedback can change interface elements, their appearance, position, or layout.

data.text: Low-fidelity prototyping uses non-digital materials rather than code, giving a quick and cheap way to test appearance and gather usability feedback. It is primarily associated with horizontal prototypes, though it can also support vertical ones. A single interface sketch captures an interface's appearance, but it cannot show interaction by itself. A storyboard uses a series of keyframe sketches to show a task's interaction and create a vertical prototype that can be evaluated and revised.
points: Low-fidelity prototyping uses non-digital materials without programming, code, or a computer.
Low-fidelity prototyping provides a quick, cheap way to brainstorm alternative designs and gather usability feedback.
Low-fidelity prototyping is primarily associated with horizontal prototypes, but can also implement vertical ones.
An interface sketch draws an interface's components, appearance, and layout, but one sketch mainly shows a horizontal prototype, not interaction.
A storyboard is a series of keyframes showing task screens and actions, forming a vertical prototype for evaluation and revision.

questions.question: What best characterizes a high-fidelity prototype?
options: paper mockups of interface appearance and layout
computer-made static interface sketches without coding
actual software development, possibly on a reduced scale
sketch-based brainstorming of alternative interface designs
questions.explanation: High-fidelity prototyping uses computer programs or programming, so it is effectively software development on a reduced scale. Static sketches, paper mockups, and sketch-based brainstorming belong to lower-fidelity methods, not to high-fidelity prototyping.

questions.question: In medium-fidelity prototyping, what makes a prototype vertical rather than horizontal?
options: real functionality added to the prototype’s screens
a longer series of paper-based mockup sketches
simulated interaction with key presses or timers
more detailed static interface sketches on paper
questions.explanation: A medium-fidelity prototype is horizontal when it only presents static interface sketches, and it can become vertical when a computer animation or slideshow simulates interaction with key presses or timers. Real functionality or low-fidelity paper series are not the medium-fidelity condition described for a vertical prototype.

questions.question: Why may making a horizontal prototype using a high-fidelity approach not make much sense?
options: medium-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes
high-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for horizontal prototypes
high-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes
low-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes
questions.explanation: High-fidelity prototyping is primarily meant for vertical prototypes, so using it mainly to produce a horizontal prototype is usually not a good fit. Low-fidelity work is primarily horizontal, and medium-fidelity work is meant for both horizontal and vertical prototypes.

data.text: Medium- and high-fidelity prototyping are contrasted by how much real software is involved. Medium-fidelity uses computers without coding and can support horizontal or vertical prototypes, while high-fidelity uses programming and is effectively reduced-scale software development. The higher effort and programming requirement make high-fidelity less suitable for horizontal prototypes, which are mainly the domain of lower-fidelity approaches.
points: Medium-fidelity prototyping uses a computer to make simple prototypes without coding; low-fidelity does not use computers or digital media.
High-fidelity prototyping uses computer programs or programming, so it is actual software development, perhaps on a reduced scale.
High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and needs much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity, requiring skilled programmers.
Medium-fidelity prototypes can be horizontal as static interface sketches or vertical with simple keypress or timer simulations.
Low-fidelity prototyping is primarily horizontal, high-fidelity prototyping is primarily vertical, so high-fidelity horizontal prototypes may not make much sense.

questions.question: In a Wizard of Oz prototype, what makes the subject experience the system as if it were autonomous?
options: A limited computer program produces the responses the subject receives
A pre-planned response script produces the responses the subject receives
A hidden human operator produces the responses the subject receives
A recorded sequence of outputs produces the responses the subject receives
questions.explanation: A Wizard of Oz prototype gives the impression of an autonomous computer because an unseen human operator creates the responses the subject receives. A program, recording, or script would be a different kind of prototype rather than the defining Wizard of Oz mechanism.

questions.question: Why can a Wizard of Oz approach support an unproven speech-recognition idea before the recognizer is built?
options: To avoid the need to gather user feedback on the idea
To replace the recognizer with a simpler final product
To prove that the recognizer already had sufficient accuracy
To test acceptability before committing resources
questions.explanation: The approach is useful when the required technology is not yet available because it lets users experience and judge the idea before development resources are committed. It does not prove final accuracy, replace the final product, or skip user feedback.

questions.question: What was transmitted to the user's screen in the IBM listening-typewriter setup?
options: The recognizer's generated transcription
The intermediary's transmitted control signals
The microphone's captured audio
The hidden operator's typed characters
questions.explanation: In the IBM listening-typewriter setup, the hidden wizard heard the user's speech and typed characters that were sent to the user's screen. A machine-generated transcription would not fit because automatic speech conversion was not yet available.

data.text: The Wizard of Oz approach makes a user believe an autonomous computer is responding, while a hidden human operator supplies the response. This can test an idea before the needed technology exists. IBM used it in a 1984 listening typewriter experiment, where a hidden wizard heard the user's speech, typed characters, and sent them to the user's screen, making the user believe conversion was automatic.
points: In the Wizard of Oz approach, a user believes an autonomous computer is acting, but a hidden human operator responds.
IBM used Wizard of Oz in 1984 to test a speech-recognition idea before speech recognizer technology was available.
In the IBM listening typewriter, a hidden wizard heard speech, typed characters, and sent them to the user's screen.

items.reason: Feasibility study, requirement gathering, and code testing are stages of the interactive system development lifecycle, whereas full implementation is a complete build of a software idea rather than a lifecycle stage.

questions.question: Why does the design-prototype-evaluate cycle in interface and interaction design need both a quickly built prototype and a quick usability evaluation method?
questions.reference_answer: The cycle can require many rounds of design, prototyping, evaluation, and refinement before the design stabilizes. Quick usability evaluation keeps the turnaround time short so those many cycles can be done without cost overrun. A quickly built prototype is also needed to model the design idea, because both are required for fast execution of the cycle.

questions.question: How does a vertical prototype differ from a horizontal prototype in the usability aspects it can test?
questions.reference_answer: A horizontal prototype shows the entire interface at a surface level, without functionality or interaction, so it is suited to feedback on look, feel, and appearance. A vertical prototype implements a few selected features in depth from the first screen to the last screen, so it is suited to analyzing interactions and features.

questions.question: Why can a series of interface sketches represent a vertical prototype while a single interface sketch represents only a horizontal prototype?
questions.reference_answer: A single interface sketch gives only a horizontal prototype because it does not show the sequence of user actions and interface changes needed to execute a task. A series of sketches forms a storyboard, where each sketch is a keyframe, a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point. The keyframes capture the sequence of user actions and screen appearances from the beginning of the task to its end, so the series can depict interaction as a vertical prototype.
